transcript:
Meeting header: 2026-10-28 15:00 UTC | Duration: 55m | Attendees: Alex Chen (Redwood AE), Jordan Patel (Redwood SE), Mei Wong (Redwood SE); Sofia Ramos, Daniel Kim, Priya Menon (HelixAI)

[00:00] Alex Chen: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, we wanted to dig into model-specific tuning for Llama, Mistral and Qwen, especially around runtime perf, batching, KV cache and the MoE routing costs. Sofia, you want to kick off with what your current constraints are?

[00:18] Sofia Ramos: Yeah, thanks. Um, primary requirements are sub-150 ms p95 for short chat prompts, and throughput of about 120 reqs/sec for our internal assistant. We're evaluating hosted vs dedicated vs private on-prem for regulatory reasons, so we need both perf and isolation.

[00:35] Daniel Kim: Also from infra side we care about GPU utilization and cost -- we ran some MoE experiments and saw routing overhead spike when batch size grows. Not sure if that's expected or our impl.

[00:50] Jordan Patel: Right, MoE routing is tricky, especially when you have many experts; there's a tradeoff between expert parallelism and cross-expert communication. For inference on our runtime we typically do top-k routing with cache alignment to reduce KV reloads.

[01:10] Mei Wong: Quick note, some of the terms might get mangled in the transcript, e.g. RoPE sometimes get transcribed as rope or R-O-P-E spelled out, and KV cache as K-V cash.

[01:22] Priya Menon: That's okay. From a network standpoint, will KV cache require additional network egress if we put the cache in a separate VPC? Concerned about latency of cross-host KV lookups.

[01:38] Jordan Patel: Good point. On Redwood runtime we co-locate KV cache in the same GPU host when possible; that avoids cross-host hops. For VPC/on-prem deployments we can run the cache in-process or as shared memory to keep p95 low. But if you have a distributed KV across nodes you will see p95 go up by 30-60 ms depending on serialization.

[02:05] Sofia Ramos: For RoPE scaling — we're experimenting with long-context prompts (up to 64k) for retrieval-augmented generation. How does RoPE scaling affect kernel selection and memory usage?

[02:20] Jordan Patel: RoPE scaling increases statefulness; our runtime switches to kernel variants optimized for long context, and we also adjust KV cache eviction policies. Practically you see more KV cache memory and longer KV lookups. Quantization can help, but watch precision drift with RoPE-scale factors; some models like Qwen seem more sensitive.

[02:43] Daniel Kim: We tried 8-bit quantization on Mistral and saw a 10% perplexity bump for certain prompts. Is that expected?

[02:51] Alex Chen: Slight degradation is common for aggressive quantization. Our recommendation: run per-model calibration and use mixed-precision quantization (8-bit for FFN, 16-bit for attention) or GPTQ-style per-channel to reduce regression. We'll share the calibration spreadsheet.

[03:12] Mei Wong: Also consider operator fusion and kernel selection; for Mistral, the fused attention kernels give you better throughput at small seq lengths, while for Llama variants the attention matmul paths can be more efficient with certain tile sizes.

[03:35] Sofia Ramos: About batching — we mostly want low-latency for interactive calls but want batching to improve cost. What's the recommended dynamic batching policy?

[03:46] Jordan Patel: Adaptive batching by latency SLO: keep a small base batch (1-4) with a short max wait (6-12 ms) and allow burst batching for background workloads. Redwood's continuous batching groups requests with similar seq lengths to avoid wasted padding. For Helix's workload, if p95 target is 150 ms, we recommend base batch 2, max batch 16, and latency cap 12 ms for batching wait. That should recover token throughput without blowing p95.

[04:20] Daniel Kim: How about MoE routing overheads when batching? We saw routing all-to-all costs add up. Any runtime tricks?

[04:29] Jordan Patel: Yes, MoE introduces a per-token routing map which can create sparsity and cause strided memory access. Tricks: combine expert routing for requests with similar routing patterns, pre-sort tokens to reduce memory jumps, and use specialized kernels that pack expert activations. But there is inherent overhead: for small batches, MoE might be slower than a dense model of similar parameter count. You pay for routing and load balancing.

[04:58] Sofia Ramos: So for our cost model, would you recommend a dense Llama 2 variant or a MoE Qwen variant?

[05:06] Alex Chen: It depends on workload. If you have high concurrency and long context, MoE's capacity can be cost-effective at scale but only if you can amortize routing overhead across large batches. For low-latency interactive workloads, dense models or smaller quantized Llama/Mistral variants often win. We can run A/B benchmarks to quantify.

[05:30] Priya Menon: On-prem specifics: we run in our datacenter with VPC-like networking. We need Redwood Private but with strict firewall and no internet egress. Is that supported?

[05:42] Alex Chen: Yes, Redwood Private supports air-gapped/on-prem deployments. We use a local control plane option and integrate with customer KMS/HSM for keys. We'll send SOC2 and network diagrams. For KV cache placement, we'll recommend colocating with model processes inside the same host, and using shared memory IPC to avoid crossing host boundaries.

[06:05] Daniel Kim: One more on RoPE: when you extend RoPE for long sequences some implementations re-scale frequencies; does Redwood's runtime handle RoPE interpolation or do we need to recompile model weights?

[06:19] Jordan Patel: We support RoPE extrapolation strategies at runtime for some model families; you may need a lightweight weight transform step for best accuracy. For Qwen variants, we recommend an offline RoPE rescale pass if you're going beyond originally trained context windows, otherwise accuracy dips.

[06:36] Sofia Ramos: Thanks. Can you summarize the recommended configuration for us to test on-prem?

[06:42] Alex Chen: Sure — for HelixAI interactive assistant targets: 1) Start with a 7B dense Llama/Mistral quantized to 8-bit with per-channel GPTQ calibration; 2) Batching: base 2, max batch 16, 12 ms wait; 3) KV cache: colocate on GPU host, use shared memory IPC; 4) If you test MoE Qwen, do large-batch throughput benchmarks and expect routing overhead; we'll help tune expert count and routing top-k; 5) RoPE: for >32k context run RoPE rescale offline for Qwen. We'll provide benchmark templates.

[07:15] Priya Menon: That helps. Security docs and SOC2 would let us move forward. Also want to see cost model for Dedicated vs Private.

[07:25] Alex Chen: We'll include cost estimates (H100 vs A100), and show expected tokens/sec and $/1M tokens.

[07:35] Mei Wong: I'll follow up with kernel trace examples and instructions for collecting perf traces on your on-prem nodes — helps us debug routing hotspots.

[07:45] Daniel Kim: Great, and Jordan, can you run a baseline with our sample prompts and the two model configs next week?

[07:52] Jordan Patel: Yep, I'll schedule the run and we can share logs in the shared folder.

[08:00] Alex Chen: Ok final recap / next steps: Alex share quantization + batching spreadsheet; Jordan run on-prem perf test and collect traces; Mei share kernel trace instructions; Priya share VPC/network details; Redwood to send SOC2 and network diagrams. We'll reconvene after results.

[08:20] Sofia Ramos: Thanks all. That was super helpful.

[08:30] Call end.
